title: Availability heuristic

definition.text: A mental shortcut that judges how likely or important something is by how easily examples come to mind.

facts.text: The easier the consequences of something are to recall, the bigger they tend to seem.
Tversky and Kahneman first studied and named it in 1973.
Wide media coverage of rare, vivid events such as homicides or airline accidents makes people overrate them compared with common diseases or car accidents.
Because recall is affected by more than real frequency, relying on it produces systematic biases.

contested_note: Critics argue that ease of recall, not the number of examples recalled, drives the effect, and that the classic studies are too vague about mental processes.

title: Bounded rationality in environmental decision making
article: Bounded rationality in environmental decision making

definition.text: The application of bounded rationality to how environmental policy decisions are made.

facts.text: Established environmental policy theory assumes homo economicus: fully rational, self-regarding people.
That assumption is troublesome because policymakers often have only an incomplete picture of an environmental problem.
All environmental actors are human, with limited cognitive abilities and incomplete information.
The more actors involved in an environmental decision, the more complex it becomes and the less predictable its outcome.
A green strategy, in line with the Porter hypothesis, uses strict rules expected to spur cleaner innovation; eco-dumping weakens rules to boost resource exports.
These two extremes try to solve many-sided wicked problems with one-sided policies.

title: Choice architecture

definition.text: The design of the ways choices are presented to people, and the effect that presentation has on what they decide.

facts.text: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein coined the term in their 2008 book Nudge.
Advocates use it to nudge people toward saving for retirement, healthier food or organ donation, compensating for decision biases.
Its tools include defaults, expecting error, feedback, structuring complex choices and incentives.
It can translate metrics into what people care about, such as turning energy use into greenhouse gas emissions.
It led to the UK's Behavioural Insights Team and a White House Nudge Unit.
Critics say it can limit choice, undermine autonomy, or raise firm profits at consumers' expense through dark patterns.
Responses differ by person; liberals and conservatives react differently to information about the environmental effects of energy use.

contested_note: Critics of libertarian paternalism argue choice architecture can impose costs on rational people and undermine autonomy, while its advocates say no presentation is neutral.

definition.text: The finding that offering many options can lower people's motivation to choose and their satisfaction with the choice.

facts.text: Classical economics predicts more options leave people at least as well off, but each option costs time and effort to evaluate.
How much it matters varies a lot between situations.
Choice architects can limit options or give decision support tools, though limiting options can reduce welfare.
